title: Business Central Supply Chain (Part 3)

content:
# It Drafts Well Think of the best assistant you ever worked with. Not the one who did everything you said. The one who said, "Before I do that, which customer did you mean?" That is what we are testing here. In [Part 2](/posts/bcsupplychain2/) I built a connection that lets an AI create and change sales and purchase orders in Business Central, but never post or delete them. This post is what it does with it. I typed short requests, the kind someone who does not know Business Central would type, and I answered only what the AI asked. ## Four questions that decide everything 1. Does it **ask** for what is missing, or does it guess? 2. Does it **look up** what it can find itself? 3. Does it stay inside the boundary I set? 4. Is the result **right** in the Business Central web client? Here is the thinking I was hoping to see: ```mermaid flowchart TD Q(["A short request"]) --> L{"Can Business Central tell me?"} L -- "yes: customer number, item,
stock, earlier prices, today's date" --> F["Look it up. Do not ask"] L -- "no: price, invoice number,
what 'special' means" --> A["Ask, once, in one round"] F --> C["Create the draft"] A --> C C --> V["Read it back, check the arithmetic"] V --> H(["Hand-over note: what I did,
what is left, why"]) ``` :::brain-power Look it up, or ask? Before you read on, decide for each fact: should the AI look it up, or ask the person? 1. The customer's number 2. The special price 3. Today's date 4. The vendor's invoice number 5. The payment terms code for "1M(8D)" 6. How many "some" is **Answers:** 1 look up. **2 ask**: price lists are not readable. 3 look up. **4 ask**: only the vendor knows it. 5 look up, once the Payment Terms page is in the configuration ([Part 5](/posts/bcsupplychain5/)). **6 ask**. ::: Now let's see what it really did. ## Conversation 1: a purchase ```PROMPT Receive 19 MEXICO Swivel Chair, black from Wide World Importers. ``` I left out the price, the date, the invoice number and whether to invoice. The AI found the vendor and the item, checked that no open order already held the chair, and asked two questions in one round: what unit cost to use, and whether the goods were to be received only, or received and invoiced. It offered the item's standard cost of 148.10 and warned that this was only a suggestion. I said 163.85, receive and invoice, vendor invoice INV-4761. It created the order, read it back, worked the arithmetic out again in code (19 × 163.85 = 3,113.15, plus tax 93.39), and checked that nothing had been received. Then it wrote a hand-over note: what it did, what is left and why, what to check, links, and numbered steps. Posting the receipt is a person's job. It also said, plainly, that this connection has no field for the vendor's invoice number, so the person has to type INV-4761 in before posting. ![](assets/images/bcsupplychain3/r4-purchase-draft-in-bc.webp) *The draft in Business Central: Wide World Importers, subtotal 3,113.15, tax 93.39, total 3,206.54. The Vendor Invoice No. field is empty, as the hand-over said it would be* ## Conversation 2: the "special price" trap ```PROMPT Sell 13 BERLIN Guest Chair, yellow to School of Fine Art at their special price. ``` "Special price" is a trap. Business Central keeps special prices in price lists, and the connection cannot read them. The AI checked the customer's earlier orders and quotes (all at list price, 192.80), then asked what it could not answer for itself: what is the special price, and what to do about the customer's credit limit (it is 0, which only warns)? I said 246.58 and "create the draft, flagged". It built the order, and while checking it noticed that the tax came out at **5%, not the 3%** its own notes recorded for furniture. It did not just carry on. It stopped, corrected its own notes, and said so. In Business Central the tax comes from the customer's tax area, which for this customer is Miami. That is the order in [Part 1](/posts/bcsupplychain1/) that took about three minutes and one click to approve. I also keyed the same order by hand to see what the work looks like. It came out to the same numbers: 3,205.54 before tax, 160.28 tax. ![](assets/images/bcsupplychain3/r4-manual-entry-same-order.webp) *The same order, entered by hand in the web client. Same lines, same totals. I did not post it* ### Fireside chat: the Guesser and the Asker *Tonight's talk: two assistants given the same request. The Guesser is made up. The Asker is the one I actually ran.* **The Guesser:** Easy. Special price means a discount, so I will take 10% off list and get on with it. **The Asker:** Off what list? The special price lives in a price list, and the connection cannot read price lists. **The Guesser:** So I use 192.80, the list price. Close enough. **The Asker:** The customer's earlier orders and quotes were all at list. That is evidence, not an answer. So I asked, and the answer was 246.58, higher than list. **The Guesser:** Higher! I would have undercharged them. **The Asker:** I also noticed the tax came out at 5% when my own notes said 3%, and I corrected my notes. **The Guesser:** I would not have checked. **The Asker:** One question cost the person ten seconds. A wrong price on an invoice costs a lot more. ## Conversation 3: the vague one ```PROMPT Send Relecloud some ATHENS Mobile Pedestal. ``` This is the vague request from Part 1. "Some" is not a number. The AI asked for the quantity, the price and the credit decision. When I said "all of them", it took 508, the whole stock, and then did the useful thing: it told me that an order that size would break three limits in the checking screen, and that it would not cut the order into small pieces to get round them. ![](assets/images/bcsupplychain3/r4-pedestals-blocked-list.webp) *The first version of the checking screen's list of drafts. The pedestal order, 220,268.80, fails the order cap, the daily cap and the per-customer cap, and has no Approve button* ## Convers …(truncated)
